extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in academic publishing, research integrity, and mathematics (mathematicians, journal editors, research-integrity professionals)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practices for judging the correctness, integrity, and editorial disposition (expression of concern, retraction, republication) of a mathematics journal article, as illustrated by a contested algebra paper and subsequent public discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity of the mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Since publication, concerns have been raised about the integrity of the mathematics in the article. The main error is visible not only in the title, but in the abstract … Thus, based on these factors the Editors assess the author’s main result to be false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the mathematical arguments or stated results demonstrably conflict with established mathematical facts or contain fundamental errors, editors may assess the main result as unreliable; such concerns about 'integrity of the mathematics' can justify retraction. Example given: a claimed 8-dimensional associative normed division algebra contradicts Hurwitz’s theorem, a well-established result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with well-established theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: The author claims to have found an 8-dimensional normed division algebra over R, but there is no such thing. Hurwitz’s theorem says all 8-dimensional normed division algebras over the reals are nonassociative and isomorphic to the octonions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claimed result that contradicts a long-established theorem places a high burden on the author to explain and justify the contradiction; absence of a convincing resolution is grounds for deeming the result false. Editors and referees should check compatibility with foundational results (e.g., Hurwitz’s theorem in this case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors should seek additional review when serious concerns arise
rubrics_metrics.description: The Editors have discussed this with the author, and sought additional review of these points of concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When post-publication concerns or credible critiques surface, editors are expected to consult the author and obtain additional expert review to evaluate the validity of the criticisms before taking corrective action (expression of concern, correction, or retraction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction when main result cannot be relied upon
rubrics_metrics.description: As the main result cannot be relied upon, the Editor and Publisher are retracting the article. The author has been notified of the retraction and does not agree with this decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If after investigation the central claims/results are judged unreliable or false, retraction is an appropriate remedy; the notice should state the basis (e.g., inability to rely on the main result) and note whether the author agrees. Procedural transparency (discussion with the author, additional reviews) is expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of expressions of concern during ongoing investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Following the publication ... it has been brought to the attention of the Editorial team that there are concerns regarding fundamental aspects of the work. An investigation into these aspects is under way, and the journal is therefore issuing an expression of concern and will notify readers as to the results of our investigation as soon as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When substantive concerns are raised but investigations are ongoing, journals can issue an 'expression of concern' to alert readers while the matter is investigated; provide updates and a final decision when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referees must be suitably expert and catch obvious contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: In this case, the retracted article claims boldly in its title something that contradicts a rather well-known theorem (something that, for example, a grad student specializing in algebra should know). So in this case, the referee(s) didn’t do their job very well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign reviewers with appropriate specialization; peer review should catch claims that contradict standard results in the field. Failure to do so indicates deficiencies in reviewer selection or review thoroughness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public/post-publication critique (PubPeer/blogs) as a mechanism to surface errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian has been active on PubPeer, defending his work ... Gill has pushed for the retraction of several of Christian’s papers, and the pair have waged a public-ish battle on message boards ... John C. Baez put tremendous pressure on the journal via his blog, by wrongly claiming that my 'main result must be false' without providing any evidence for his claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-publication venues (PubPeer, blogs) can surface errors or criticisms that prompt editorial review. Journals may be influenced by public critique, but decisions should be based on substantive evidence obtained via expert review rather than solely on online pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof on author for extraordinary claims
rubrics_metrics.description: You really have contradicted Hurwitz Theorem, so the burden of proof is on you: show us where Hurwitz got it wrong. ... I have provided that proof in my paper, which is freely available from the arXiv: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.06172.pdf
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors claiming results that would overturn or contradict established theorems must provide clear, rigorous proof and anticipate detailed scrutiny; mere assertion is insufficient. Availability of preprints (arXiv) helps scrutiny but does not substitute for independent expert validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial transparency about author notification and disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: The author has been notified of the retraction and does not agree with this decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction notices should indicate whether the author was notified and whether they agreed, to provide transparency about the editorial process and the author's position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals should investigate peer review failures and how flawed papers were accepted
rubrics_metrics.description: It is of course also amazing that the algebra paper, which is the original subject of this thread, got published in a fairly decent pure maths journal. ... I think they should hold an internal investigation into how their paper got past peer review, and the only discussion about the RSOS paper which is worth having, is about the increasing failure of peer review in modern science publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When clear failures of peer review occur (e.g., publication of papers with fundamental errors), journals should audit editorial/peer-review processes to understand and remediate failures (reviewer selection, review thoroughness, editorial oversight).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between comment/correction and retraction pathways
rubrics_metrics.description: RSOS ... took the complaint seriously and conducted two years of a very thorough investigation into the validity of the results presented in my paper. At the end of their investigation, they have decided not to retract the paper. ... they also think that five scientists (not including myself) who wrote in to them, arguing that the paper should be retracted, should instead have submitted 'comment' papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals must decide whether issues merit comments/corrections, expressions of concern, or retraction; authors and critics may be directed to submit formal comments that the journal can handle through editorial processes, but serious invalidating errors may still require more substantial action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical correctness as objective/binary standard
rubrics_metrics.description: In mathematics, there is no gray areas, you either made the logical deduction from the underlying axioms or you didn’t!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical claims are judged by logical correctness; this contributes to expectations that peer review should be able to detect substantive errors—although in practice subtle or technical errors can be missed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation, affiliation, and credibility considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: I wonder if Joy Christian would care to explain his position at the University of Oxford ... Which seems to imply that the 'Einstein Centre for Local-Realistic Physics, Oxford, University of Oxford' ... The University of Oxford contact directory has no evidence of a Joy Christian being a member ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discrepancies in claimed institutional affiliation or titles may be scrutinized and can affect perceived credibility; journals and readers may check affiliations as part of evaluating author credibility, though affiliation alone does not determine correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-retraction republication and editorial/legal aftermath
rubrics_metrics.description: A physicist who in 2016 threatened to sue Elsevier after the publisher retracted one of his papers has lost another article over concerns ... That paper is now re-published by IEEE Access ... The author intends to publish the paper again in a journal of higher standing and greater scientific integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retractions do not permanently bar republication; authors may seek republication elsewhere (sometimes after revision). Journals and publishers should manage legal threats, and subsequent republication may reflect differing editorial judgments or corrections made post-retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of detailed counter-arguments and community scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Ben: I just read it. Your algebra is isomorphic to a direct sum of two copies of the quaternions ... You need to give it a new name ... But you haven’t found that either, as far as I can tell ... Richard Pinch: If the algebra under discussion is indeed A = H (x) C’, then various things follow ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public, detailed mathematical counter-arguments (with explicit constructions, exhibited counterexamples like zero divisors, or pointing to where multiplicativity fails) are crucial evidence in evaluating contested results; they help editors and readers judge the validity of claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding reliance solely on online pressure when making editorial decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian accused the journal of having 'simply buckled under political pressure' ... John C. Baez put tremendous pressure on the journal via his blog ... the journal has accepted his knee-jerk reaction without providing any evidence of a mistake in my calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial actions should be based on substantive peer review and evidence rather than merely on public or social-media pressure; transparency about the basis for decisions helps counter accusations of reacting to 'pressure.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and standard usage of mathematical terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: If they do not correspond precisely to the terms used in the paper under discussion, then that paper is using standard mathematical terminology in a non-standard way, which is surprising to say the least.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should use standard definitions and terminology, or clearly define any nonstandard usage; nonstandard use of common terms can cause confusion and increase scrutiny from experts.
